newsitem.title: USA: Soybean, grain prices rise, coffee and lumber fall.
newsitem.headline: Soybean, grain prices rise, coffee and lumber fall.

text.p: Soybean prices rose on Wednesday on talk of exports to China, while corn and wheat prices closed higher on worries about spring flooding.
In other markets, coffee and lumber prices fell and oil prices were mixed. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Index of 17 futures prices closed up 0.41 point at 244.75.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed 8 cents a bushel higher at $8.39 as China was rumored to have bought 50,000 metric tons of soybeans for April shipment.
Due to clogged ports, China had recently backed off buying U.S. grain, with newly harvested South American soybeans also providing stiff competition for sales to China.
So the rumored sale, which U.S. exporters did not confirm, was still deemed a positive sign for demand.

Also positive for soybeans was the concern about expected flooding in the Corn Belt this spring after the winter's heavy snowfall. Grain prices soared in 1993 during a "hundred year flood" of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers.

"New crop (months) got support on potential flooding in the upper Midwest," said Goldenberg-Hehmeyer grain analyst Bob Lekberg. "That did more for corn, but the bean market has to stay competitive as farmers make planting plans."
May wheat closed up 7-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.91, with traders citing concerns that the expected flooding in the upper Midwest could delay spring wheat plantings.
May corn closed up 2-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.03-1/4, with concerns centered on possible flooding delaying corn planting and forcing a shift of planned corn acreage to soybeans.
Corn is planted before soybeans in the heart of Midwest grain belt stretching from Ohio to Nebraska.

On Wednesday the Clinton Administration asked Congress for $2 billion in emergency aid for natural disasters that have already occurred this winter including flooding of the Ohio River and tornadoes in the South.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, May lumber futures closed down the allowable $10 daily limit at $395.50 per thousand board feet as traders ignored a strong housing construction report this week and focused on weak cash prices.

Cash markets showed only a brief period of demand after Tuesday's February U.S. housing starts report, despite starts surging 12.2 percent from a month earlier at the fastest pace of building in three years.
"Despite a bullish housing report we have a pathetic cash market and that is what affected futures all day," said Curt Cunningham, President Pacific Futures Trading.
Traders cited worries about a flood of fresh Canadian wood shipments after April 1, when a fresh year of exporting under a bilateral timber agreement starts.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures shrugged off a strike threat by Colombian port workers. May coffee closed down 0.70 cent a pound at 168.10 cents.

Futures rose briefly when a union official said dock workers at Buenaventura, Colombia's main Pacific coast port and the shipment point for 60 percent of the country's coffee exports, could strike in less than a month to protest port operators' failure to fulfill the terms of a January accord.

A nine-day dockworkers' strike in January disrupted coffee exports from the world's second-largest producer and heightened supply concerns at a time when inventories were near 20-year lows. Prices rose to 2-1/2 year highs.

But since then supply worries have eased as producers took advantage of higher prices and moved more coffee into exchange warehouses. Warehouse stocks rose for the tenth day in a row on Tuesday, reaching 64,529 132-pound bags.
"The market will react to it when it happens," Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said of the Colombia news.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline and heating oil prices closed higher but crude prices edged lower after late selling by speculators ahead of the expiration on Thursday of April futures contracts.
April crude oil ended two cents a barrel lower at $22.04 after rising as much as 59 cents to $22.65.

Refined products rose after a weekly report from the American Petroleum Institute showed larger-than-expected drawdowns in stockpiles. U.S. stocks of gasoline fell 4.3 million barrels when traders expected supply to be steady.
April gasoline closed up 0.48 cent a gallon at 67.96 cents and April heating oil up 0.11 cent a gallon at 56.29 cents.
